solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Stood up one woman for another

blocks.note: Rose is the past tense of rise, to stand up.
Mary is a woman's name.

explanation.surface: Someone was jilted on a date as one partner was swapped for another.
explanation.walkthrough: "Stood up" reads as being jilted, but it is simply the past of rise; the two women are MARY and the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by context: after "one woman", "another" means another woman's name, and Rosemary is one.

clue.text: Better luck next time with export of Parma?

blocks.note: A British phrase of mock sympathy for bad luck.
Parmesan, named after Parma, is the Italian city's famous export; the question mark flags it as one example of a type.

explanation.surface: A commiseration to an Italian exporter whose shipment has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: HARD CHEESE! is British slang said to someone out of luck; Parmesan is a hard cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: an idiom of offhand commiseration, and a definition by example since Parmesan is one hard cheese.

clue.text: Blooming beech is rid of what does for weeds

indicators.note: A blooming tree changes shape as it opens, so the letters open out into a new order.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A gardener notes that a flowering beech has been cleared of weedkiller.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rid" looks like part of the definition (rid of weeds) but it belongs to the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: "does for" is British informal for kills, and weedkilling chemicals are exactly that.

clue.text: Swimmer is pale

blocks.note: 's is the short form of is.
Wan means pale.

explanation.walkthrough: "Is" reads as a link word but supplies the S, as in "it's".
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the swan is a bird that glides on water, so it is one kind of swimmer.

clue.text: Press club

blocks.note: The verb, as in smoothing creases out of clothes.
A golf club with a metal head.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a journalists' club; both words go separately to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a plain synonym for pressing clothes flat, and a definition by example for the golf club.

clue.text: Girl is left behind

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left.
Ass is American slang for the backside.

explanation.surface: A girl has been abandoned while others moved on.
explanation.walkthrough: "Left behind" reads as one phrase meaning abandoned, but it splits into two parts: left and behind (the bottom).
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, chiefly Scottish and northern English, for a young woman.

clue.text: Fashionable fiction over university instead

blocks.note: In means fashionable.
A lie is a fiction.
U is the standard abbreviation for university.

explanation.surface: Trendy novels are taking the place of a university education.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, "over" puts the first pieces above U.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from French, where lieu means place: in place of.

clue.text: Accordingly fabric provides comfort

blocks.note: So means accordingly.
Lace is a fabric.

explanation.surface: A statement that soft cloth is therefore comforting to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fabric provides comfort" reads as a sentence about clothes; comfort is the noun defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: consolation offered to someone in distress.

clue.text: With a standard accent “isn’t” commonly gets slap

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with.
Used as printed.
RP, Received Pronunciation, is the standard British accent.
Ain't is the colloquial form of isn't.

explanation.surface: Someone speaking the Queen's English says ain't and gets slapped for it.
explanation.walkthrough: "Slap" is not a blow but British theatrical slang for make-up; RP (Received Pronunciation) is the accent once taught as standard British English.
explanation.definitionFit: Two slang words for the same thing: both jokingly mean heavily applied make-up.

clue.text: Blokes starting to distribute remedy

blocks.note: Blokes are men.
First letter of distribute.

explanation.surface: Men begin handing out a cure.
explanation.walkthrough: Remedy is a verb here, not the noun the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to put something right.

clue.text: Clowns fall for such a cuckoo family?

blocks.note: Bananas means crazy, cuckoo.
Kin is family.

explanation.surface: Circus clowns are charmed by an eccentric family.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fall for" reads as being charmed; here it is literal slapstick, slipping over.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the fruit peel is the classic slapstick trap that sends a clown sprawling.

clue.text: Destroy dead tree

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for dead.
An ash is a tree.

explanation.surface: An order to fell a dead tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Destroy is meant in the sense of ruining hopes, not felling timber.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the idiom of dashed hopes: to wreck or shatter.

clue.text: Done in like the house after umpteenth encore?

definitions.text: like the house after umpteenth encore

blocks.note: British slang for exhausted.

blocks.clueFragment: like the house after umpteenth encore
blocks.note: The house is the theatre audience, whose hands are tired from applause.

explanation.surface: A theatre audience is exhausted after calling the performers back yet again.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is whimsical: an audience that has applauded through countless encores has literally worn itself out applauding.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: British slang for worn out, and a literal reading for an audience that can applaud no more.

clue.text: First character to appear in Aristophanes?

definitions.text: First character to appear in Aristophanes?

blocks.note: Reads as the first person on stage, but means the first letter.
The playwright wrote in Greek, and his name in Greek letters starts with the same letter as it does in English.

explanation.surface: A question about which figure walks on first in one of Aristophanes' comedies.
explanation.walkthrough: "Character" suggests a role in a play by the Greek dramatist, but it means a letter of the alphabet: the Greek A that opens his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the first letter of the Greek alphabet, and the first of Aristophanes' name.

clue.text: A form of kinkiness?

blocks.note: Per means a, as in "ten pounds per head" for "ten pounds a head".
A version is a form of something.

explanation.surface: Asking whether something counts as a type of kinky behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: "A" looks like a throwaway article, but it supplies PER.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: abnormal sexual behaviour, which kinkiness describes.

clue.text: Plongeur shared wish disastrously

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A kitchen hand's joint hope goes badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Plongeur is the French kitchen term for the person who washes up.
explanation.definitionFit: A translation: the French restaurant word for the kitchen hand who washes the pots and plates.

clue.text: Weepy hardly holds back effusive promo

indicators.note: The two words hold the answer inside them.
The held letters are read backwards.

blocks.note: wEEPY Hardly contains EPYH.

explanation.surface: A tearjerker film barely holds back from gushing publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters span the gap between the two words, running backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: extravagant, gushing publicity.

clue.text: With superintendent I’d be an absolutely marvellous trickster

definitions.text: With superintendent I’d be an absolutely marvellous

blocks.note: One who fools people.

blocks.clueFragment: With superintendent I’d be an absolutely marvellous
blocks.note: A superintendent is a SUPER; the answer tacked on after it makes a rhyming phrase meaning absolutely marvellous.

explanation.surface: A con man boasts that with a senior police officer on side he'd be brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: SUPER plus the answer gives super-duper, slang for absolutely marvellous.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: one who dupes, a plain synonym for trickster, and the second half of super-duper.

clue.text: Problem with old form of wrestling

blocks.note: A sum is an arithmetic problem.
O is the standard abbreviation for old.

explanation.surface: A complaint about an outdated style of wrestling.
explanation.walkthrough: Problem is a maths problem, not a difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Japanese style fought by heavyweights pushing each other from a ring.

clue.text: She often ditches mates with long hair at hospital department

blocks.note: A mane is a long head of hair.
Used as printed.
ER, the emergency room, is a hospital department.

explanation.surface: A long-haired woman at a hospital department keeps dumping her partners.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs up to "mates"; "with" joins it to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A description of the informal sense: a woman who takes lovers and then discards them.

clue.text: Dessert with own scent?

blocks.note: Afters is British informal for dessert.
To own is to have.

explanation.surface: A pudding that comes with its own aroma.
explanation.walkthrough: Afters is British slang for the pudding course.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the lotion men splash on after shaving is a kind of scent.

clue.text: Rip off a winter warmer?

blocks.note: To swindle or overcharge, as a sheep is shorn.
A warm jacket of soft synthetic pile.

explanation.surface: Asking whether a cosy winter garment should be torn off.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rip off" is not tearing but overcharging.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: slang for swindling someone, and a definition by example for the warm jacket.

clue.text: What Sooty waved with ‘elp?

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with.
Help is a hand; dropping the H as 'elp does gives 'AND.

explanation.surface: A question about what the puppet bear Sooty flourished while calling for help.
explanation.walkthrough: Sooty is a British children's TV glove puppet who performs magic tricks; the dropped H in 'elp tells you to drop it from HAND too.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the magician's stick Sooty waved with his catchphrase "Izzy wizzy, let's get busy".

clue.text: These may let slip men’s states

definitions.text: These may let slip men’s states

indicators.note: The letters slip out of place.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.

explanation.surface: Official checks might reveal people's financial circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: the checks expose (let slip) people's financial states.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes checks on income before benefits are granted, which reveal a person's financial state.

clue.text: Shipbuilder is someone who’s well aware, we hear

indicators.note: We are told how it sounds, not how it is spelt.

blocks.note: One who knows; in a British accent that drops the final R it matches the name.

explanation.surface: A boatbuilder is praised as someone who knows his stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: The match relies on a British accent that drops the final R of KNOWER.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Old Testament patriarch who built the Ark.

clue.text: Ship a blown instrument

blocks.note: A tub is a slow, clumsy ship.
Used as printed.

explanation.surface: A request to send off a wind instrument that has been blown.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ship" looks like a verb, to send, but it is the noun: a tub.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the large, low-pitched brass instrument played by blowing.

clue.text: Pace set by flipping family favourites

indicators.note: Flipping turns the word end over end.

blocks.note: Family pets are favourites; a pet is a favourite person or animal.

explanation.surface: A tempo chosen by switching between a household's best-loved songs.
explanation.walkthrough: "Flipping" might pass for a mild British curse; its job is to turn PETS around.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a single stride when walking.

clue.text: Racket in returning laptops, say

indicators.note: Returning sends the word back the way it came.

blocks.note: Macs are an example of laptops, which "say" signals.

explanation.surface: A fraud involving laptops being sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: "Say" marks MACS as an example of laptops, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the criminal sense: a dishonest money-making scheme.

clue.text: Jostle for top slot – to wit, witter on

blocks.note: SC, short for Latin scilicet, means to wit.
To witter on is to ramble.

explanation.surface: Rivals competing for the top job talk on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: SC (scilicet) is the Latin abbreviation meaning namely; witter is British for talking at length about nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a disorderly struggle to grab a position ahead of others.

clue.text: Intro of noble with name entered

blocks.note: O is a short form of of, as in o'clock.
A peer is a noble.
N is the standard abbreviation for name.

explanation.surface: The start of a nobleman's introduction once his name has been recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: "Of" looks like a link word but supplies the O.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: whatever starts things off, such as the first item in a show.
